summary: This proposed standard states that when a DNS resolver receives an NXDOMAIN response, it means that the name and all names under it do not exist. It clarifies RFC 1034 and modifies part of RFC 2308, updating both.

plainLanguage.summary: If the answer to whether a street exists is no, then none of the houses on that street exist either. This makes that rule clear for the internet's phone book.

subtitle: If a DNS name does not exist, nothing underneath it exists either, and resolvers should cache it that way.

tldr.problem: Most resolvers treated a cached NXDOMAIN as proof only for the exact name asked about, because RFC 1034 was ambiguous about empty non-terminal names versus nonexistent ones. Queries for names below a nonexistent name were still sent to authoritative servers.
tldr.mechanism: An NXDOMAIN response means the denied name and every name beneath it do not exist. An iterative caching resolver SHOULD cache it and answer later queries for any descendant name with NXDOMAIN, without asking again.
tldr.outcome: Caches become more efficient and authoritative servers see less pointless traffic. The RFC is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 1034 and RFC 2308.

today: RFC 8020 is a Proposed Standard and, according to the metadata for this site, has not been obsoleted or updated. It updates RFC 1034 and RFC 2308.

sections.title: The Ambiguity Being Fixed
sections.content:
The DNS defines response code 3 as Name Error, better known as NXDOMAIN: the queried name does not exist. Because domain names form a tree of labels, a node that does not exist cannot have a subtree. The iterative resolution algorithm already treats it that way and stops as soon as an authoritative server returns NXDOMAIN.

Caches did not. In most known resolvers, a cached nonexistence was not treated as proof that no child names exist. The RFC blames an ambiguity in RFC 1034 that failed to separate Empty Non-Terminal (ENT) names from nonexistent names. DNSSEC made the distinction important, and RFC 4035 explains how authoritative servers make it, but no RFC described the behavior for recursive servers.
sections.plainLanguage: Asking a librarian for a shelf that does not exist should also tell you that no books on that shelf exist. Computers were forgetting that and asking about every single book.

sections.title: The NXDOMAIN Cut Rules
sections.content:
When an iterative caching resolver receives an NXDOMAIN response, it SHOULD store it in its cache. All names and RRsets at or below that node SHOULD then be considered unreachable, and later queries for such names SHOULD get an NXDOMAIN answer. The RFC calls this the NXDOMAIN cut.

There are exceptions. A resolver that already holds cached data under the cut MAY keep sending it until its TTL expires. A validating resolver MAY apply the cut only when the NXDOMAIN response was validated with DNSSEC. The nonexistence is not forever: the negative TTL from RFC 2308 still limits how long it is cached.

For signed zones, the same NSEC or NSEC3 records that prove the original name does not exist also prove it for descendants. The resolver MUST return them when the triggering query had the DNSSEC OK (DO) bit set.

If there is a chain of CNAME or DNAME records, the name that does not exist is the last name of the chain, not the QNAME. The cached NXDOMAIN is for that denied name.
sections.plainLanguage: Once the map says there is no such town, the helper writes it down. When someone asks about a street in that town, the helper answers right away instead of checking again. The note is thrown away after a while, in case the town gets built.

sections.title: What It Changes in RFC 1034 and RFC 2308
sections.content:
For RFC 1034, the document clarifies the ambiguity about ENTs. ENTs are nodes with no resource record sets of their own that have descendants which do. The correct response for an ENT is NODATA (a response code of NOERROR with an empty answer section), not NXDOMAIN.

For RFC 2308, it rewrites the second paragraph of Section 5. A cached NXDOMAIN can now be returned for another query for the same QNAME and QCLASS, or for a query whose QNAME is a descendant of the original QNAME with the same QCLASS.
sections.plainLanguage: Two old rulebooks were a bit vague, so this one adds a clear sentence to each: a no for a place is also a no for everything inside it.

sections.title: Benefits
sections.content:
The main benefit is better cache efficiency. Take a nonexistent foo.example. Many resolvers forward a query for foo.example and then another for bar.foo.example. With the NXDOMAIN cut, the second is answered from the cache, so authoritative servers have less unnecessary traffic to process.

The behavior works well with QNAME minimization (RFC 7816), because the resolver can stop searching as soon as it meets an NXDOMAIN. It may also help against random QNAME attacks, where queries have a fixed nonexistent suffix and a random prefix. With the cut, an administrator only needs to send the resolver a query for the fixed suffix, and the resolver stops forwarding the rest.

The benefit is limited: if the first query is for bar.foo.example and the second for baz.foo.example, the first answer says nothing about baz.foo.example, so the second query is still sent.
sections.plainLanguage: If the school says there is no Room 9, you do not need to ask about Room 9 shelf one, then shelf two. One answer saves lots of trips.

sections.title: Possible Issues
sections.content:
Two problems are noted. First, a private setup can break. If the TLD example exists but foobar.example is not delegated, an administrator might still run an internal zone office.foobar.example by making the local resolver forward that zone to local servers. Depending on query order, the resolver might cache the nonexistence from example and effectively delete everything under it. The RFC assumes such setups are rare and need not be supported.

Second, some authoritative servers answer an ENT with NXDOMAIN instead of NODATA. The RFC says such servers are wrong and always have been, and that their behavior is incompatible with DNSSEC. Given the advantages of the cut, there is little reason to support that.
sections.plainLanguage: If someone secretly built a house on a street the map says does not exist, the helper might say the house is not there. The RFC says that kind of secret house is rare, so it is not worth worrying about.

sections.title: Implementation Notes
sections.content:
This section of the RFC is non-normative. A resolver that keeps its cache as a tree can follow the rules by pruning the subtree of positive cache entries at the NXDOMAIN node, or by deleting every cache entry below it. When searching downward, it then stops at a cached nonexistence.

Some caches are not trees (a dictionary, for example), so they have a reason to ignore the rules. That is why the rules use SHOULD and not MUST. The tree is a model for reasoning: implementations may use any data structure.

Appendix A explains one thing resolvers must not do. The owner name of the SOA record in an NXDOMAIN reply marks the apex of the zone, not the closest existing name, so it cannot be used to deduce a cut. A cut is recorded only for the denied name.
sections.plainLanguage: It does not matter whether the helper keeps notes in a tree-shaped chart or a list, as long as the answers come out right. That is why the rule says should, not must.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The technique may help against the denial-of-service attack called random QNAMEs, described in the benefits section.

There is also a downside. If a resolver does not validate with DNSSEC, or the zone is not signed, the resolver can be poisoned with a false NXDOMAIN, which deletes part of the domain name tree. That attack is already possible without this RFC, but the NXDOMAIN cut may increase its effects. The RFC says the only solution is to use DNSSEC.
sections.plainLanguage: A trickster could tell the helper that a whole town does not exist. Only a signed, checkable answer can stop that trick.
